steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Step-Back Prompting, a prompting technique that has LLMs first abstract to high-level concepts and principles before reasoning. Motivate it from the difficulty of multi-step reasoning, explain the abstraction-and-reasoning idea, and summarize the main results and analyses.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLM revolution: Transformers, scaling, emergent abilities
- Multi-step reasoning still hard; existing remedies; our proposal
- Abstraction as a human cognitive skill; two-step abstraction-and-reasoning
- Experiments and headline results
- Analyses: comparison with CoT/TDB, error analysis

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Natural language processing (NLP) is going through a ground-breaking revolution because of Transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Scaling up the model size and the pre-training corpus brought remarkable improvements in model capabilities and sample efficiency, with insights from the scaling law, and also emergent abilities like multi-step reasoning and instruction following.

Even with these big advances, complex multi-step reasoning is still challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs. Prior work shows that process-supervision with step-by-step verification is a promising remedy to make intermediate reasoning steps more correct. Techniques like Chain-of-Thought were introduced to produce a coherent series of intermediate reasoning steps, to increase the success rate of following the right decoding path. When humans face challenging tasks they often step back and do abstractions to get to high-level principles that guide the process. Inspired by this, we propose Step-Back Prompting, which grounds reasoning on abstractions to reduce the chance of making errors in the intermediate reasoning steps.

Among many cognitive skills, abstraction is ubiquitous to how humans can process vast amounts of information and derive general principles. For example, Kepler compressed thousands of measurements into Kepler’s three laws of planetary motion, which precisely describe how planets orbit around the Sun. In critical decision-making humans find abstraction helpful because it gives a broader view of the environment. This work explores how LLMs can tackle complex tasks with many low-level details through a two-step process of abstraction-and-reasoning. In the first step we show LLMs how to step back through in-context learning, prompting them to derive high-level abstractions such as concepts and principles for a specific example. In the second step they use their reasoning ability to reason on top of the high-level concepts and principles. We use few-shot exemplar demonstrations to execute Step-Back Prompting on LLMs.

- Experiments
  - tasks: Physics, Chemistry reasoning; knowledge-intensive QA; multi-hop commonsense
  - up to 27\% in PaLM-2L; Figure 1 summary
  - TimeQA, MuSiQue: PaLM-2L and GPT-4 only \sim 40\%
  - CoT minor; Step-Back 7\% / 11\% MMLU Physics / Chemistry, 27\% TimeQA, 7\% MuSiQue
- Analyses
  - up to 36\% over CoT and “take-a-deep-breath” (TDB) prompting
  - fixes up to \sim 40\% errors, max \sim 12\% new
  - most errors from LLM reasoning limits; abstraction easy to demonstrate

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Natural language processing (NLP) is going through a ground-breaking revolution because of Transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Scaling up the model size and the pre-training corpus brought remarkable improvements in model capabilities and sample efficiency, with insights from the scaling law, and also emergent abilities like multi-step reasoning and instruction following.

Even with these big advances, complex multi-step reasoning is still challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs. Prior work shows that process-supervision with step-by-step verification is a promising remedy to make intermediate reasoning steps more correct. Techniques like Chain-of-Thought were introduced to produce a coherent series of intermediate reasoning steps, to increase the success rate of following the right decoding path. When humans face challenging tasks they often step back and do abstractions to get to high-level principles that guide the process. Inspired by this, we propose Step-Back Prompting, which grounds reasoning on abstractions to reduce the chance of making errors in the intermediate reasoning steps.

Among many cognitive skills, abstraction is ubiquitous to how humans can process vast amounts of information and derive general principles. For example, Kepler compressed thousands of measurements into Kepler’s three laws of planetary motion, which precisely describe how planets orbit around the Sun. In critical decision-making humans find abstraction helpful because it gives a broader view of the environment. This work explores how LLMs can tackle complex tasks with many low-level details through a two-step process of abstraction-and-reasoning. In the first step we show LLMs how to step back through in-context learning, prompting them to derive high-level abstractions such as concepts and principles for a specific example. In the second step they use their reasoning ability to reason on top of the high-level concepts and principles. We use few-shot exemplar demonstrations to execute Step-Back Prompting on LLMs.

We run experiments on a range of tasks with domain specific reasoning like Physics and Chemistry, knowledge-intensive question answering that needs factual knowledge, and multi-hop commonsense reasoning. We see significant performance improvements (up to 27\%) in PaLM-2L, which shows that Step-Back Prompting is effective for complex tasks that are otherwise challenging because of the amount of details needed for reasoning. Figure 1 shows a summary of all the key results in this paper. Some of the tasks are very challenging: PaLM-2L and GPT-4 both get only \sim 40\% accuracy on TimeQA and MuSiQue. Chain-of-Thought prompting gives a minor improvement on a few tasks, while Step-Back Prompting improves PaLM-2L across the board: 7\% and 11\% on MMLU Physics and Chemistry, 27\% on TimeQA, and 7\% on MuSiQue.

We do a variety of analyses and find that Step-Back Prompting gives strong performance improvements (up to 36\%) over chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and “take-a-deep-breath” (TDB) prompting. In a qualitative evaluation we find that Step-Back fixes a large part of the errors of the base model (up to \sim 40\%) and introduces only a small part of new errors (max \sim 12\%). We also do an error analysis and find that most of the errors of Step-Back Prompting come from the intrinsic limitations of the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, while abstraction skills are relatively easy to demonstrate to LLMs, which points to the direction for future improvements of methods like Step-Back Prompting.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The field of natural language processing (NLP) is witnessing a ground-breaking revolution because of Transformer-based [1] large language models (LLMs) [2,3,4,5]. Scaling up the model size and pre-training corpus [6,7] has brought remarkable improvement in model capabilities and sample efficiency, with insights from the scaling law [8,6], as well as emergent abilities [9] such as multi-step reasoning [10,11] and instruction following [12,13].

Despite these great advancements, complex multi-step reasoning remains challenging for even state-of-the-art LLMs. [14] show that process-supervision with step-by-step verification is a promising remedy for improving the correctness of intermediate reasoning steps. Techniques such as Chain-of-Thought [10] were introduced to produce a coherent series of intermediate reasoning steps and increase the success rate of following the right decoding path. Inspired by the fact that humans, when faced with challenging tasks, often step back and do abstractions to arrive at high-level principles that guide the process, we propose Step-Back Prompting to ground reasoning on abstractions and reduce the chance of making errors in the intermediate reasoning steps.

Among many cognitive skills, abstraction [18] is ubiquitous to humans’ ability to process vast amounts of information and derive general principles. For example, Kepler compressed thousands of measurements into Kepler’s three laws of planetary motion, which precisely describe the orbits of planets around the Sun [19]. In critical decision-making, humans find abstraction helpful since it provides a broader view of the environment. This work explores how LLMs can tackle complex tasks involving many low-level details through a two-step process of abstraction-and-reasoning. The first step is to show LLMs how to step back through in-context learning, prompting them to derive high-level abstractions such as concepts and principles for a specific example. The second step is to leverage their reasoning ability to reason on top of these high-level concepts and principles. We use few-shot exemplar demonstrations to execute Step-Back Prompting on LLMs.

We experiment across a range of tasks involving domain specific reasoning such as Physics and Chemistry, knowledge-intensive question answering requiring factual knowledge, and multi-hop commonsense reasoning. We observe significant performance improvements (up to 27\%) in PaLM-2L [5], demonstrating the efficacy of Step-Back Prompting in tackling complex tasks that are otherwise challenging due to the amount of details needed for reasoning. Figure 1 summarizes all the key results presented in this paper. Some of the tasks are very challenging: both PaLM-2L and GPT-4 achieve only \sim 40\% accuracy on TimeQA and MuSiQue. Chain-of-Thought prompting leads to a minor improvement on a few tasks, while Step-Back Prompting improves the performance of PaLM-2L across the board: 7\% and 11\% on MMLU Physics and Chemistry, 27\% on TimeQA, and 7\% on MuSiQue.

We conduct a variety of analyses and find that Step-Back Prompting leads to strong performance improvements (up to 36\%) over chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting [10] and “take-a-deep-breath” (TDB) prompting [20]. In a qualitative evaluation, we find that Step-Back fixes a large portion of the base model's errors (up to \sim 40\%) while introducing only a small portion of new errors (max \sim 12\%). We also conduct an error analysis and find that the majority of errors made by Step-Back Prompting are attributable to the intrinsic limitations of LLMs' reasoning capabilities, while abstraction skills are relatively easy to demonstrate to LLMs, pointing to the direction for future improvements of methods like Step-Back Prompting.
